title: Bechet sits in with James Reese Europe's band
summary: Braud tells how Europe and Noble Sissle heard Bechet and Bechet outplayed twelve clarinetists; he then contrasts bop with Dixieland and Ellington rhythm.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Sidney Bechet: the man, the horn, the legend

blocks.x: I was playing at the Mantis in 1917. James P. Europe from New York came then with his band, the 15th. That was one of the, at that time, they were one of the finest military bands I ever heard. And he had 12 clarinet players. So he came in the ducks and he listened to Sidney. So he called Sidney over to the table, him and Noble Sisson of New York. And he asked Sidney to join his band. Would he join his band? Can Sidney join his band? He said, well, Mr. Europe, he said, I don't read. He said, I'd like for you to come to my rehearsal down at the Carla Sims. And so he accepted the engagement. So he asked me, he says, bro, come on down to me. I'm going to hear the 15th band. I said, you might enjoy that. So I said, yeah, okay. So we went on down. He did. At that time, they played, uh, Fortin Pleasant. So, he listened. So Mr. Europe asked him would he like to sit in after hearing his concert numbers. So he said, yes, I'll sit in. And he sat in. And there's a clarinet cadenza in closing plastic. And when that guy got through playing the cadenza, well, uh, Jim Europe 12 clarinet players couldn't come on. Because they hadn't heard anything. That's what I tell you about soul. The man got soul. He got the feeling and the phrase and everything that goes. You know what I mean? He's a real artist. And he's like myself. He's very sensitive. If something isn't going wrong, I'm in a section, a rhythm section, if something going wrong, it'll drag me. You know what I mean? You got to drag me. Because you've been used to hearing one beat and you hear something else. You know, if you take the piano players today or the drummers of today, they're coming up with what they call bop and progression. Well, that doesn't fit in Dixieland at all. It tears you up. And I had the opportunity to run them kind of fellas that said they was a piano player, but they never played chord. See what I mean? Everything was bop. Well, it doesn't make sense in a Dixieland band because you're a customer of hearing chords. Well, we'll go back to Ellington band, fuller chords. Fuller chords and rhythm. Ellington band, if the saxophone players had what we call a lick chorus, the brass wasn't sitting down there, as we call them in New Orleans soldier, soldier in the band. They play a lot of rhythm. And if the brass had a lick chorus, well, the saxophone would play rhythm. You know what I mean? The feeling. You know what I mean? Rhythm. But the man didn't write that, of course not. He didn't have that written, but it just comes from soul. You take fellas like Barney Bigger, Johnny Hodges, Arthur Hardrick, they're great. Conny.
